name: Grace Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing management and accounting, in Nottingham. My week is lectures from nine to four on three days, tutorials, and flashcards at the kitchen table in the evenings. I do volleyball on Thursdays, and I go home to my parents' house on some weekends.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you choose accounting, and how is it going so far?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad's a dentist and he says people always need a professional with a clear qualification. Accounting felt solid and sensible. It's going well, I got the top mark on the first assignment, but I also read the news and I'm wondering if I've chosen a job a machine does. My parents pay everything, so no debt at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I thought: the tools do small jobs and people exaggerate. I'd tell friends that accounting still needs people who can sign things off. I'd feel a bit vindicated, and I'd keep it quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still worry about getting a good graduate place. There are only so many at the big firms, and everyone with top marks applies. Even a small automation of routine checking means fewer entry jobs, and I'm the kind of person who'd notice every one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd sit the first professional exam as early as I can, apply for a placement year, and keep my marks near the top. I'd also work on my interview skills, because I'm better on paper than in a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My family is fine for money, but I carry the fear of getting it wrong. It's my own worry, not the world's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by getting it wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What do you mean by getting it wrong? Choosing the wrong course, the wrong firm, the wrong city. I'm the sort of person who rereads an email four times. I'd rather be sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How would you change that? Probably by talking to people who are a few years ahead. My cousin's a trainee at a mid-size firm and says it's less scary than it looks. I'd ask her to introduce me to her team. I'm the sort of person who rereads an email four times, because I'd rather be sure than be quick.

say: I'd say it's **what I expected**: small jobs done, a lot of exaggeration.
I'd tell friends accounting still needs people to **sign things off**.
think: I still worry about **graduate places**, because routine checking jobs shrink a little.
My fear of **getting it wrong** is my own, not the world's.
do: Sit the first **professional exam** early and apply for a placement year.
Practise **interviews**, because I'm better on paper than in a room.
feel: **Uneasy**: money is fine, but the fear of a wrong choice never leaves.
S0.quote: I'm the sort of person who rereads an email four times, because I'd rather be sure than be quick.
fieldNote: Grace's unease holds even in the mildest world: it comes from **perfectionism**, not from AI.
She names her gap, interviews, and plans to fix it with her cousin's help.

steps.text: Apply for a placement year at a mid-size accounting firm
Sit the first professional exam as early as possible
Ask my cousin to introduce me to her team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what everyone has been saying and now it's real. I'd tell my friends accountants will still be needed, but the work will look different. I'd say it calmly, though I wouldn't feel calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. Checking, reconciling and filling in forms are what junior accountants do, and those are exactly what the card says goes first. If the big firms hire half as many trainees, my top marks stop being enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I can control. I'd ask my lecturers which skills firms will still pay for, probably advice and judgement. I'd go to the careers office, and I'd try one of the tools in a lecture where the teacher shows us, not alone. I wouldn't start with tools I'd trust blindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can't see an obvious fix, and I'm someone who wants one. I'd also feel annoyed that nobody gave us a warning when we chose courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should have warned you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who do you think should have warned you? The university, the professional bodies, the firms. They all say there's lots of opportunity, and I'm 18 and trusting them. I'd like them to say what they're actually seeing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a lecturer said the tools are safe to use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do if a lecturer said the tools are safe to use? I'd try, slowly, with a small task and I'd check every answer. I wouldn't hand over a whole assignment. The firms, the university and the professional bodies all say there's plenty of opportunity, and I'm 18 and I trusted them.

say: I'd tell friends accountants will still be needed, but the **work will look different**.
I'd say it calmly, though I wouldn't feel calm.
think: Checking and reconciling are **what juniors do**, and those go first.
If firms hire **half as many** trainees, top marks stop being enough.
do: Ask lecturers which **skills firms pay for** and visit the careers office.
Try one AI tool on a **small task** in class and check every answer.
feel: **Anxious**: she wants a fix and can't see one, and feels no one warned them.
S1.quote: The firms, the university and the professional bodies all say there's plenty of opportunity, and I'm 18 and I trusted them.
fieldNote: Grace's fear is **specific**: junior reconciliation and checking work is the very work in the card.
She wants institutions to tell the truth, not to reassure her.

steps.text: Ask lecturers which accounting skills firms will still pay for
Visit the careers office about firms' hiring plans
Try an AI tool on one small task in class and check it
Keep my marks near the top

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's terrifying, and that no one is ready. I'd go to my tutor, my parents and the university and ask what happens to my degree. I wouldn't post anything online, because I'd rather not look scared in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'd chosen the wrong thing. I'd be a second-year in 2028 when AGI arrives, and accounting would be one of the first jobs to go. I'd lie awake thinking about whether to stop, to switch, or to wait, and I can't make a risky decision on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my parents and a student adviser what the options are, and I'd probably stay on the course until someone gave me a better one. I'd start learning the tools finally, because if the whole thing is that big then avoiding them is pointless. I'd also keep my savings in cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's a constant background panic. I'd be fine for money, but I wouldn't know what I was for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is knowing it's two years different from the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How is knowing it's two years different from the others? There's no time to think. In the slower worlds I'd spend a year deciding, and in this one I'd have to decide in a week and be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want to happen? Someone in charge, like the government or the profession, telling us clearly: finish, switch, or wait. I'd follow a clear instruction before I'd trust my own guess. I'd rather follow a clear instruction from the government or the profession than trust my own guess about something this big.

say: I'd say it's **terrifying** and no one is ready, but only to tutors and parents.
I wouldn't post it online, because I'd rather not look **scared in public**.
think: I'd have chosen **the wrong thing**, in a job that goes first.
I can't make a **risky decision** alone, so I'd lie awake over it.
do: Ask a tutor and adviser whether to **finish, switch or wait**.
Start learning the tools finally, and keep savings in **cash**.
feel: **Alarmed**: constant background panic, and unsure what she is for.
S2.quote: I'd rather follow a clear instruction from the government or the profession than trust my own guess about something this big.
fieldNote: Grace is **alarmed** because her chosen job goes first and her resistant style leaves her without a plan.
Money isn't the issue; purpose is. She wants someone in authority to tell her what to do.

steps.text: Ask my tutor and a student adviser whether to finish, switch or wait
Start learning AI tools with a lecturer's help
Stay on the course until I have a better option
Keep my savings in cash and accessible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious, but we've got time to see it coming. I'd tell friends to ask their courses for a plan. I'd probably be the one in the group asking the tutor what happens after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's still frightening, but different. I'd finish my degree in 2029 and might get two years of work before AGI. That feels like a short career, but it's something. I'd have savings and a family behind me, which is more than many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, but add skills that will still matter, like advice, tax planning, working with clients and getting comfortable with the tools. I'd try a placement year, save money, and maybe study another subject like psychology on the side. I'd decide each year, not all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way that I can live with. It's the sort of worry that gets me working, not the sort that freezes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't? A chance to change my mind with some information. I can wait a year and see what the profession says, and not guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most about those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What worries you most about those years? That I'll spend them waiting for someone to tell me what to do, and that no one will. I know that's a habit of mine and I'd like to break it. I'm worried I'll spend those five years waiting for someone to tell me what to do, and that nobody will.

say: I'd say it's serious but we have **time**.
I'd ask my tutor and my course leader what the plan is for students after **2031**.
think: I'd finish in 2029 and might get **two years of work** before AGI.
I have **savings and family**, which is more than many.
do: Add **client advice** and tax planning skills, and try a placement year.
Decide **each year** instead of all at once, and save.
feel: **Anxious**, but the kind that gets her working rather than freezing.
S3.quote: I'm worried I'll spend those five years waiting for someone to tell me what to do, and that nobody will.
fieldNote: Grace works best with **time and information**: five years lets her revise a choice without gambling.
She names her own habit of waiting for instructions.

steps.text: Add client advice and tax planning skills to my accounting degree
Take a placement year and save most of what I earn
Review my course choice with a tutor each year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and I'd stay steady. I'd tell friends to learn what they can and not worry too much about the date. I'd also say that the profession will change, but it won't vanish overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel safer. By 2036 I'd be 28, qualified and perhaps a manager. I'd have time to adapt in small steps, which is how I prefer to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do my qualifications, and learn the tools gradually once they're settled. I'd save steadily and I'd keep an eye on how the firms change. I'd also learn something that doesn't depend on a screen, like running a small team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but low. It's like knowing the weather will turn in a few years: you buy a better coat when you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be resistant to the tools ten years from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you still be resistant to the tools ten years from now? Probably a bit, yes. But I'd rather be late and sure than early and wrong. I'd learn them when everybody else has made the mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at 18 in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell the 18-year-old you in this world? To stop rereading every email four times. I'd say you've got ten years, you won't run out of time, and you can afford to try something. I would rather be late and sure than early and wrong, so I'd learn the tools after everyone else has made the mistakes.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long time**, so I'd stay steady.
The profession will **change, not vanish** overnight.
think: By 2036 I'd be **28 and qualified**, maybe a manager.
I'd have time to adapt in **small steps**, which suits me.
do: Finish the degree and **qualifications**, then learn tools once they are settled.
Learn to **run a small team** and save steadily.
feel: **Uneasy**, but low, like buying a better coat before the weather turns.
S4.quote: I would rather be late and sure than early and wrong, so I'd learn the tools after everyone else has made the mistakes.
fieldNote: Grace's unease **drops sharply** with time, because small steps are her way of changing.
She would remain slow with tools but treats that as a method.

steps.text: Finish the degree and sit the professional qualifications
Save steadily from my first salary
Learn AI tools gradually once they are settled

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one scares me most. I'd be in the middle of my degree and I wouldn't know whether to carry on. What would help is clear advice from the profession, which says what accountants will do, and a guarantee that finishing my degree isn't pointless.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I know I'm slower with technology than my friends and I'd rather admit it. I'd like someone to explain these things to me calmly, and not as though I'm behind. I picked accounting because it felt safe and sensible, and now I can't tell if I picked the safest job to lose.

headlineQuote: I picked accounting because it felt safe and sensible, and now I can't tell if I picked the safest job to lose.
portrait: **Grace** is an 18-year-old management and accounting student in Nottingham, with her parents, a dentist and a home-maker, paying everything.
She writes **flashcards by hand**, never uses AI tools, and chose accounting because her father said it was safe.
She sits in the **political centre** and wants clear advice from the profession, not slogans from either side.
She worries even when nothing changes, and moves to **anxious, then alarmed** at the two-year warning.
Her cushion is strong, but she lacks a plan, and her **dislike of risk** keeps her from trying new things.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be mid-degree in a job machines could do.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **clear advice** from the profession and calm help to catch up with technology.
